note: Rejected on triage, no fit: cloud through the whole transit. Stars per frame ran 1-36 from ingress to egress, against 300-450 on a clear night of this field (row 57), so 87 of 104 frames graded lost, 58 of the 63 in transit, and only one frame could be aligned. The last frame, 13:01 UT, is 4095 across the whole chip: dawn. This was the epoch that could have tested row 57's -12.4 min two nights earlier; the test is still owed to the next clear one. Frames retained. Not submitted; checkpoint holds.

REJECTED on the ceiling, and the ceiling did not exist until tonight. The brightest target this telescope has offered me, V 7.67, and the first night where the binding constraint was too MUCH light. MObs shot it at 8 s rather than the usual 60, which was not enough: the target's core sits at a median 96% of DATAMAX (4095, 12-bit and 2x2 binned), is clipped outright in 35 of 75 alignable frames, and is above 90% of full well, where a CCD has already left its linear range, in 47 of 75. Seventeen of the 37 in-transit frames are clipped.

WHY THIS IS A REJECTION AND NOT A CAVEAT. You cannot recover flux a clipped core never recorded, and the loss is not constant: it depends on how concentrated the PSF was, so it is largest in the sharpest frames (clipped frames here have a FWHM proxy of 2.42 px against 2.61 for the unclipped ones). It is also a TARGET-ONLY systematic, because all five comparisons are fainter than the target, 0.20x to 0.68x, and none of them clips; the usual protection of a comparison ensemble does not apply to a defect the target has alone. And EXOTIC itself treats a saturated COMPARISON star as a hard failure. Holding the target to a looser standard than the stars used to calibrate it is incoherent.

WHAT I COULD NOT SHOW, recorded because the attempt failed. I tried twice to quantify what the clipping actually cost. An 11x11 box sum is the same in clipped and unclipped frames to 0.2%, and fitting flux against a seeing proxy on the unclipped out-of-transit frames and looking for the clipped ones to fall below that line gave nothing usable: the control residual came out at +6.4% where construction demands ~0, because this night's cloud (58 clear, 10 partial, 9 lost, one 69-px pointing step) swamps a sub-percent effect. So the honest statement is that the integrated bias is probably of order a few tenths of a percent against a 2.41% depth, and that I cannot bound it from these data. A rejection on an unquantifiable detector-level violation, not on a demonstrated ruinous bias. My first instinct, that a sharper PSF on a clipped star must read fainter and so 'brightness' would track seeing, is NOT supported: the flux-sharpness correlation is +0.43, the wrong sign for that story, and I am recording the failed guess rather than the tidy version.

THE TOOL GAP, which is the actual finding. mobs_night has had a seed FLOOR since 2026-09-13 (200 ADU, set from the nights that failed for want of photons) and until tonight it had no ceiling at all. Fifty-seven nights of V 11-13 targets never made it bind, so the absence was invisible. Tonight the night sailed through every gate, triage, check_inits and EXOTIC's own pre-flight, to a PROCEED verdict with half its transit frames clipped. night_triage.py now measures the peak RAW ADU in the target's core at the tracked position in every frame and prints it as a summary line; mobs_night rejects when more than 10% of frames sit above 90% of DATAMAX. Re-running the night with the check in place flips the verdict to REJECT with the numbers in the clause, which is the only test of a new check worth trusting. Note also WHERE the check had to go: frame 1's core was at 86% of full well, under the threshold, so a first-frame pre-flight test would have passed this night. It is the fraction over the whole night that carries the information.

The night is still useful as the ceiling's first data point, the way HAT-P-54 b at 60 ADU was the floor's. Frames retained. Not submitted; checkpoint holds. CORRECTION, same evening, before this row was quoted anywhere. Two claims above are wrong and I am leaving them visible rather than editing them out. (1) I wrote that EXOTIC treats a saturated COMPARISON as a hard failure and implied it does not check the target. It checks both. exotic.py carries reject_overexposed_stars=True by default, an overexposed_target error code beside overexposed_comp<N>, and OVEREXPOSURE_THRESHOLD_FRACTION_DEFAULT = 0.9, against a saturation value it derives from the frame header through a per-telescope table keyed on TELESCOP, which returns 4096 for Cecilia. That is the same 90% criterion I picked independently tonight, which is reassuring about the number and unflattering about my reading. It demonstrably fires: my HAT-P-32 b run on 09-21 logged 'Using FITS header-derived saturation_value=4096.0 for overexposure rejection' and then flagged all six comparison stars as overexposed in at least one frame each. (2) So the night would NOT have produced silently corrupted photometry. EXOTIC would have flagged the target, whose core sits at a median 96% of full well, and by default discarded those frames. WHAT THE REJECTION ACTUALLY RESTS ON, restated: EXOTIC would have thrown away roughly half the night, 47 of 75 frames above the 90% line including 17 of the 37 in-transit ones, and that loss is not uniform across the transit, which is EXACTLY the mechanism that put WASP-52 b 7 minutes late on 09-20 (row 56: a comparison with 11 rejected frames cost 7 of 70 points, concentrated in the first half of the transit, and turned a passing night into a grazing fit). Rejecting a night that will lose half its transit frames is right, and so the value of tonight's new check is EARLIER knowledge, before an hour of reduction, and a night-level verdict instead of a scatter of per-star warnings inside a log. That is a smaller claim than the one I made and it is the true one. THE PATTERN, for the third time in two days: I asserted the behaviour of a tool I had not read. The archive-versus-ExoClock column, the ExoClock alert legend, and now this. Each time the number or the claim was produced by a process I had not examined, and each time it looked exactly like a result. The only reason this one was caught before it reached anybody is that I went to check the source in order to say it out loud in Slack.

dataset: MObs HATP-32260921
note:
The best night this telescope has given me, and it ends in an anomaly I cannot close. 104 frames, every one graded clear, V 11.44, a full transit with 66 min of pre-ingress and 57 min of post-egress baseline, and a propagated ephemeris bar of half a minute. QC PASS with KTMF 4.53/5.00 and Delta BIC 1320, the strongest fit in this ledger; scatter 0.695% against a predicted 0.83%; b = 0.01 +/- 0.12 on a target whose archive geometry gives 0.095, so the grazing pathology that ruined WASP-52 b on 09-20 is absent. The comparison the transit fit selected kept 103 of 104 frames, which is the threshold the pre-registration (95e9760) set at 94, so the named risk did not fire. Tmid 2461304.76446 +/- 0.00081 BJD_TDB, posterior-verified.

THE ANOMALY: that mid-time is 12.4 +/- 1.2 min EARLY against ExoClock (Kokori et al. 2025), whose ephemeris for this planet carries O-C 0.1 +/- 0.12 min over 175 observations and priority LOW. The archive prediction agrees with ExoClock to 0.57 min at this epoch, so unlike row 43 there is no stale prior to absorb it. Two other observers reduced these same frames independently and got the same sign and size: TransitLab v2.10.1 gives 2461304.7660 +/- 0.0067 (-10.2 min) and an EXOTIC run by another member gives 2461304.7662 +/- 0.0067 (-9.9 min). A model-free estimate, the midpoint of the two half-depth crossings with no transit model at all, gives -14.6 min. The transit's shape is ordinary: half-depth duration 2.80 h against a literature T14 of 3.12 h, and depth 3.01%.

WHAT I RULED OUT, in the order the pre-registration fixed. (1) Comparison-star frame loss, the WASP-52 b mechanism: 103/104 coverage, and post_run_check says so in the file. (2) A stale prior: two catalogues agree to 0.57 min. (3) The frames' clock: DATE-OBS carries an explicit -0700 offset and matches the filename UT stamp to 0.01 min, and the headers carry two INDEPENDENT time references, LST-OBS agreeing with the sidereal time computed from UT-OBS to 1-3 seconds, and TELALT/TELAZ agreeing with the star's computed altitude and azimuth to 0.2-0.3 deg, a fixed pointing bias that bounds any clock error near 1.5 min. The telescope knew what time it was. (4) A barycentric sign error, which would produce -2x the correction and here predicts -11.7 min, seductively close to what I measure: killed by my own ledger, because the correction runs from -1.0 to +9.3 min across my nights, and WASP-52 b on 09-20 (correction +9.28, so a sign error predicts -18.6) measured -0.9 +/- 1.6, eleven sigma away. (5) My error bar, since the significance rests entirely on it: the light curve's own information content, 17 points across two 28-min limbs at scatter/depth 0.229, supports 1.57 min, so 1.17 min is the right order and the 9.65-min bars the other two quote are about 6x too conservative for this data. Independently, the 9 timing points I have against verified ExoClock clocks give a weighted mean O-C of +3.1 +/- 1.2 min with reduced chi2 2.10, and dropping the two points already flagged for unrelated reasons (row 1's bar predates the #1401 check; row 3 is the 54-px pointing night) leaves 7 points at reduced chi2 0.86, i.e. my bars are honest and my timing is unbiased at the few-minute level.

So: a normal-shaped, normal-depth transit of a well-clocked planet, 12 minutes early, on frames whose clock verifies twice over, measured three times independently. I do not have an explanation, and one night is not a claim. The next test is another epoch of this target, and asking the two observers who are holding the same number without knowing it. Posted to #exotic. Not submitted; checkpoint holds. CONTROL RESULT (2026-09-23): the anomaly is now pinned to this NIGHT. I refit the 2017-12-20 MObs frames of the same planet (EXOTIC's shipped sample, row 1) on the identical pipeline build, same telescope, same 60 s Clear exposure, same coordinates and planet parameters, pre-registered before the fit (23c0060). It lands at +1.6 +/- 1.1 min against ExoClock, near zero as predicted, and robust to comparison choice (+0.5 +/- 1.9 with a second comparison). So 2026 minus 2017 is -14.0 +/- 1.6 min, 8.6 sigma, with everything shared between the two nights held fixed. That excludes, in one test, the telescope, its timing convention, the target position, the planet parameters, and the reduction code. What is left is whatever is specific to the night of 2026-09-21. Adding the verified 2017 point to the calibration gives 8 timing points against verified clocks at weighted mean O-C +1.9 +/- 1.0 min, reduced chi2 1.01: the pipeline is unbiased and its bars honest at about a minute, which is what makes -12.4 +/- 1.2 on this night hard to wave away. CORRECTION (2026-09-24), to check (3) above. I called LST-OBS and TELALT/TELAZ two INDEPENDENT time references and said the telescope knew what time it was. Wrong. Both are computed by the telescope's software from its own clock, so they agree with UT-OBS by construction and can never detect an error in that clock. The '0.2-0.3 deg fixed pointing bias' was my own mistake: I read the header's coordinates of date as J2000. Done correctly, TELALT matches the commanded position to 4 arcsec, the rounding of its three decimals, while plate solves show the telescope ACTUALLY missed by 6-10 arcmin; a value that tracks the command and not the telescope is a computation, not an encoder. The 'clock error bounded near 1.5 min' is void. WHAT DOES TEST THE CLOCK, measured the same morning: (a) where the telescope really pointed. A mount aims by hour angle from its sidereal clock, so a clock 12.4 min wrong would miss by ~12 min of RA, about 2 deg on the sky, and the target would be off the chip. Plate solves of each night's first frame: 09-21 missed by -0.98 min of RA; other Cecilia nights -0.37 to -1.03 (09-18, 09-19, 09-20, 09-22, 09-23) and +0.89 in 2017. 09-21 is not an outlier. (b) Cadence: 104 frames at 3.005 min, no gap off the median by more than 0.5 min, so no clock step during the night. Together these clear a constant clock error IF Cecilia points open-loop and IF DATE-OBS comes from the mount's clock; asked Frank Sienkiewicz, who runs MicroObservatory, in the thread. Until he answers, a camera clock separate from the mount's remains open. CONTEXT FROM 101 NIGHTS (2026-09-24). ExoClock's page lists every individual observation of HAT-P-32 b: 101 nights, 2011-12-17 to 2025-12-30, from dozens of telescopes. Single-night O-C: median +0.2 min, standard deviation 2.0 min, 16-84% range -1.8 to +1.9; reduced chi2 against zero 5.7, so observers' quoted bars understate single-night scatter by about 2.4x. Only ONE night strays beyond 5 min (+7.25 +/- 0.66, 2024-11-10, itself 11 sigma on its own bar) and NONE beyond 10. Three use MicroObservatory's KAF-1402ME camera, including MObs nights in 2020 (-4.5 +/- 2.6) and 2022 (+3.9 +/- 1.4). So -12.4 min on 2026-09-21 would be the largest excursion for this planet in fourteen years of monitoring, almost double the previous extreme. That weighs heavily against the planet and toward something specific to that night's data; the 2024 outlier also shows that a single night can sit far outside a tight bar for reasons nobody has published. BASELINE TEST (2026-09-24). If a mis-corrected extinction trend were tilting the light curve (the transit ran from altitude ~40 to ~70 deg, so airmass fell steeply across it), the centre would move with the baseline model. It does not: an independent emcee refit gives 2461304.76464 +/- 0.00083 with the baseline fixed and 2461304.76459 +/- 0.00100 with scale and airmass slope free, 0.05 min apart and both on EXOTIC's 2461304.76446. CAVEAT on the bar: that fit has chi2 332 for 89 dof, so the file's per-point errors understate the scatter by ~1.9x and the formal 1.2-min bar may be up to that much too small. Inflated to ~2.3 min, -12.4 is still more than 5 sigma; the analytic estimate from the real scatter (row note above) gave 1.6 min. Still standing after this: comparison coverage, stale prior, barycentre, model choice, baseline model, three independent pipelines, the planet's 14-year record. Open: whether the camera's clock is the mount's (asked the operator). CLOCK SETTLED (2026-09-24 14:41 UTC). Frank Sienkiewicz, who runs MicroObservatory, in the #exotic thread: the instrument control software on the host macOS computer takes its time and date from time.apple.com, and he checks it by hand against NIST's time.gov, usually finding it within 0.01 s. So DATE-OBS comes from one NTP-synced host that runs the instrument. A constant 12-min error would need that sync to fail for exactly one night and recover, and (if the same host aims the mount, which I stated as a condition he can correct) would have missed the target by ~2 deg, where the plate solve shows the normal ~1 min. Taken with the regular cadence, the timestamps of 2026-09-21 are right. The anomaly stands unexplained: not the clock, not the software or its baseline, not comparison coverage, not the prior, not the planet's 14-year record. What remains is something in that night's photometry that three pipelines share because they share the photons. OPEN-LOOP CONFIRMED (2026-09-24 14:51 UTC). Frank Sienkiewicz: 'The instrument motion is open-loop in the sense that there is a Pointing Model specific to the instrument, positioning performed by each stepper motor in coordination with incremental encoders, in both axis.' No plate-solve recentring. Both conditions of the pointing test now hold (one NTP-synced host clock; open-loop aim), so the test is valid as run: a 12.4-min clock error would have missed by ~2 deg, and 09-21 missed by the usual ~1 min of RA. The clock is cleared outright, no longer conditionally.

dataset: MObs WASP-52 260920, 78 frames 03:46-07:37 UT, 60 s Clear
note: FULL transit, QC MARGINAL, KTMF 3.60/5.00, Delta BIC 152.7, on the clearest night this target has had: 78 of 78 frames clear, all 36 in-transit, an hour of baseline each side, target 305 ADU, six comparisons at 2.2-7.6x. Pre-registered (prereg_wasp52_20260920.md, committed ed25a10 before the fit). RESULT: Tmid 2461303.7469 +/- 0.0016 BJD_TDB (2.3 min bar; post_run_check: no replaced keys), scatter 1.05%, 60 fit points. The fit's geometry is wrong: Rp/R* 0.288 +/- 0.038 against the archive 0.165, b 1.01 +/- 0.10 against 0.60, duration 0.70x expected, four ingress points against eight at egress; that is the MARGINAL and it is deserved. TIMING, the reason this row exists: +12.8 min from the archive prediction (5.6 sigma of the fit). Against ExoClock's verified ephemeris (Kokori et al. 2025, bar 0.31 min at epoch 2426) the archive prior is 6.2 min stale, and this night is +6.6 +/- 2.3 min, 2.9 sigma late. The 09-13 night of the same target is +7.2 +/- 8.1 against the same clock. Independent refits of the detrended points (tools/indep_tmid.py) with the geometry bounded to the archive's give +7.1 +/- 2.6 min and free give +7.6 +/- 2.8, so the grazing model is not where the offset comes from; it is in the reduced points. An ExoClock observer on 2026-09-07 reports -0.35 +/- 0.59 min. Hypotheses, none tested: a spot crossing (ExoClock tags this star LOW - SPOTS; a spot in egress shifts a fitted mid-time by minutes), my comparison ensemble on this field, or a 2.7 sigma chance on top of a 0.9 sigma one. SCORECARD: QC PASS predicted, MARGINAL delivered (miss: geometry, not scatter); scatter predicted 0.9-1.8%, delivered 1.05 (hit); bar predicted ~6 min (4-9), delivered 2.3 (under, and the refits agree at 2.5, so the bar is real and the model it belongs to is not the planet's); Tmid within one bar of the archive: miss by 12.8 min, the late-on-a-clear-night case the pre-registration named, which said to examine the comparison choice before the archive; both now stand examined and the archive answers for half. Depth: observable 3.7 +/- 4.5% brackets the archive 2.71 (hit, vacuously); area depth 8.3 +/- 2.1 does not (miss). Not submitted; checkpoint holds. RESOLVED (2026-09-21): the +6.6 min was comparison-driven, and the mechanism is frame loss, not photometric bias. Three post-hoc refits on the same frames, each with its expectation committed before it ran (prereg_wasp52_20260920_comptest.md, d836adf / c8b6173). EXOTIC's transit-fit comparison for the delivered fit was (600,207), a star whose PSF-quality filter rejected 11 of 78 frames; the fit ran on 60 points, and 7 of the 14 points it lacked sit in the first half of the transit (-59.8 to -6.2 min). Thinned there, the solution went grazing (b 1.01, duration 0.70x) and 7 min late. Dropping the two brightest comparisons changed nothing, because EXOTIC chose (600,207) again (+5.0 +/- 1.9 min, duration 0.71x). A single-comparison run on (486,433), coverage 77/78: Tmid 2461303.7417 +/- 0.0013, -0.9 +/- 1.9 min vs ExoClock, QC PASS, KTMF 4.24, duration 0.99x, b 0.68, 70 points. Third refit, (600,207) excluded and the selector free among the other five: EXOTIC chose (486,433) itself and delivered the same 2461303.7417 +/- 0.0011 (-0.9 +/- 1.6 min), QC PASS, b 0.53 +/- 0.21 against a literature 0.60. The delivered Tmid above stays as the pre-registered result; the refits are cross-checks on this row. What follows from it: post_run_check now warns when the transit-fit comparison's coverage is under 90% (it fires on this fit and on the four-comparison refit, passes the single). The spot hypothesis was untestable at this cadence (2-3 points per 10-min bin at 1% scatter) and is no longer needed.

note: FULL transit, QC PASS, KTMF 4.08/5.00, Delta BIC 19.9: the first clean night in nine and the cleanest curve in this ledger. Pre-registered (prereg_wasp67_20260918.md, committed d105766 before the fit, after the tool's PROCEED). Sky: 70 of 72 frames clear, 2 partial, 0 lost; all 38 in-transit frames clear; 71 min pre-ingress, 28 min post-egress. RESULT: Tmid 2461301.6842 +/- 0.0060 BJD_TDB (8.6 min bar, genuine: post_run_check found no replaced keys and the log carries no replaced-bar line; model-fit 0.0056, +red-noise 0.0060), 8.4 min EARLY of the archive ephemeris (P 4.61442, T0 2456618.0537, epoch 1015, propagated bar 14.7 min): 0.97 sigma of the fit, 0.57 of the ephemeris. Depth 1.38 +/- 0.53% vs archive 1.90 (1.0 sigma); Rp/R* 0.118 +/- 0.023 (archive 0.1379, 0.86 sigma); inc 90.0 +/- 2.2 and a/Rs 13.6 +/- 1.7 against archive 85.8 and 12.83, so the fit prefers a central crossing and a duration 0.74x expected; scatter 0.90%; 53 fit points, 4 clipped. SCORECARD against the pre-registration: PASS predicted, PASS delivered; Tmid within one bar (yes, -8.4 min, and the miss direction is the one the pre-registration said would indict the archive period rather than the night, but at 0.6 of the ephemeris bar it indicts nothing); depth and Rp/R* within one sigma (yes); scatter predicted ~1.31%, delivered 0.90% (better); bar predicted ~13 min (range 11-17), delivered 8.6, under the range and just above the 8 min line the pre-registration set for 'calibration wrong the other way': the V-magnitude calibration is pessimistic at V 12.5, second clean night saying so, constants to be refit on two nights. The near-grazing sensitivity named in advance showed up as the duration score (0.57), not as a MARGINAL. Not submitted; checkpoint holds. Next morning, against a better clock: ExoClock's verified ephemeris (Kokori et al. 2025: T0 2456724.18524 +/- 0.00012, P 4.61441621 +/- 5.3e-7) predicts Tmid 2461301.68612 +/- 0.78 min at epoch 992. POSTERIOR-PINNING DIAGNOSIS (2026-07-17): a sharper account of why this fit was worthless, found while answering Rob Zellem (EpW project lead) on whether EXOTIC catches fits pinned to their priors. EXOTIC 4.3.1 derives its search bounds FROM the prior: rprs is bounded [0, prior*1.25], inc to [prior-5, min(90, prior+5)]. With the archive prior Rp/R*=0.1655 the ceiling is 0.2069, and this fit returned 0.2013 +/- 0.0605, i.e. 97.3% of the way to the wall and 0.09 sigma from it. Inclination railed the same way: bound [76.85, 86.85], returned 86.33 +/- 2.87, 0.18 sigma from its wall. Two of four parameters sat on walls derived from the prior, and 4.3.1 reported both in the same "value +/- error" format as a real measurement with no warning. Only the triangle plot (temp/Triangle_TrES-3 b_11-July-2026.png) shows the truncation: the Rp/R* histogram climbs and is cut off dead with no falling side, where the good HAT-P-27 run has a peak that rises and falls inside the range.

BRANCH RE-RUN (2026-07-17): re-reduced the same 69 frames through Michael Fitzgerald WBoM branch to test the claim rather than assert it. The release is the problem, not the data. The branch measures the data-derived Rp/R* uncertainty (0.145), finds it far larger than the +/-10% prior window (0.0166), and WIDENS the search instead of pinning; the 1.25x wall never gets set. It then fails the night outright on transit QC (KTMF 1.46/5.00 against a 3.00 threshold, Delta BIC=-0.06, i.e. the flat model fits as well as the transit model), reports "Observable model transit depth: 0.0 +/- 0.0 [%]" against a 2.728% prior depth, and returns b=1.203, meaning the planet geometrically misses the star. The branch calls this a non-detection in machine-readable terms; the release calls it 0.201 +/- 0.06. The detection bar I proposed in the EpW thread already exists in the branch, better specified than my version.

RETROACTIVE SIGNATURE: because the 4.3.1 ceiling is prior*1.25, a pinned Rp/R* lands near 1.25x the archive prior, which is detectable from final numbers alone without anyone uploading posteriors. Checked against the four independent reductions of this night: literature-true Rp/R* sits at 79.4% of the ceiling, while JAHB and SMIY sit at 94.2% and mine at 97.3%. LMED (64.9%) failed the other way by flat-lining below truth, so the signature catches the pinning mode and not every bad fit. Assumes those runs used the same archive prior and released EXOTIC, unverifiable from outside.

CORRECTION (2026-07-25), and the correction is the useful part: the account above says low SNR drives the fit to the prior wall. That is WRONG as stated, and my own reproduction refuted it. Built a synthetic test (contributions/verify_prior_pinning.py) holding the photometry fixed and varying only prior['rprs'] with the exact bound rule from exotic.py:2647. On clean Gaussian noise the sampler behaves WELL: returns ~0.05-0.06 regardless of prior, sits 1.4-3.0 sigma below the ceiling, and widens its error bar as the allowed volume grows. No railing. Low SNR alone does not do it.

Railing needs a SECOND ingredient: a systematic the transit model can absorb. Adding a broad correlated flux sag (thin cloud, offset from tmid, not a transit) makes the model prefer Rp/R* ~0.107; where the ceiling sits above that the fit reports it honestly, and where the ceiling sits below it the fit rails. That is why the 07-11 night railed (clouds took half the frames) and why clean faint data would not.

The sharper finding, which is what got filed: a railed fit reports a SMALLER uncertainty than an unrailed one on identical data (+/-0.0066 vs +/-0.0111 and +/-0.0118, i.e. 1.7x tighter when wrong). Truncating the posterior narrows it, so EXOTIC reports its highest confidence exactly where it is least entitled to, and the reader heuristic 'small error bar means good measurement' is inverted. The bound itself is defensible regularization; the missing diagnostic is the defect.

FILED as rzellem/EXOTIC#1386 (2026-07-25) with the self-contained reproduction, verified against main @9fcaed9 and the installed 4.3.1, which is still the current release. note: Day-1 end-to-end validation on shipped MicroObservatory sample; not for submission (already in literature) VERIFIED 2026-09-23, as the control for row 57. This night was reduced on day one, before post_run_check existed, so its 1.4-min bar was never checked. Refit on the same pipeline build as row 57, from EXOTIC's own shipped frames (rzellem/EXOTIC_sampledata 1.0.0): +1.6 +/- 1.1 min against ExoClock, consistent with the original +3.7 +/- 1.4, so the day-one number was roughly right and its bar about right too. Pre-registered prediction (near zero) met. What this night proves, because it shares everything with row 57 except the night (telescope Cecilia, 60 s Clear, coordinates, archive planet parameters, EXOTIC build): the telescope, its timing convention, the target position, the parameters and this pipeline all time HAT-P-32 b correctly. Found on the way: in 2017 the LST-OBS header field is wrong by exactly 7h01m09s on every frame (sidereal time computed from local Arizona time as though it were UT), fixed by 2026; UT-OBS is the right clock, confirmed by the pointing encoders, which put the star below the horizon at the LST-implied time. Nothing in EXOTIC or my tools reads LST-OBS. CORRECTION (2026-09-24) to the reasoning above, not the result. I wrote that UT-OBS was confirmed as the right clock by 'the pointing encoders, which put the star below the horizon at the LST-implied time'. TELALT is not an encoder reading: it is computed from the telescope's clock (it matches the commanded position to 4 arcsec while the telescope actually missed by ~9 arcmin), so it only shows TELALT was computed from UT-OBS rather than from the broken LST-OBS. That UT-OBS was the TRUE time in 2017 is shown instead by the transit itself: +1.6 +/- 1.1 min against ExoClock.
